articles.title: New handmade lock gates installed at Rochdale Canal in Manchester
articles.excerpt: Handcrafted oak gates have been craned into place at Lock 80 on the Rochdale Canal, replacing gates over 25 years old.
articles.content_html:
New handmade oak gates have been craned into place at Lock 80 on the Rochdale Canal, marking a significant upgrade to the historical waterway. The gates, crafted in Yorkshire, weigh between 1,500 kg and 2,500 kg each and replace those installed over 25 years ago.

This installation is part of a broader initiative by the Canal and River Trust to restore lock gates across Greater Manchester's canal network. The project is crucial for maintaining the functionality of the canals, which are vital for local transport and recreation.

A spokesperson for the Canal and River Trust stated, "The new locks are critical to keeping canals open," highlighting the importance of this restoration work.

This project is one of hundreds planned over the next five months to maintain the 2,000-mile canal network across England and Wales.

The Rochdale Canal, which opened in 1804, is one of the first trans-Pennine canals, connecting Manchester to Sowerby Bridge in West Yorkshire. The recent installation follows similar work completed in February 2026 in Manchester's Gay Village, demonstrating ongoing efforts to preserve the region's waterways.

articles.title: Prime Minister Andy Burnham supports reinstatement of Heywood express bus service
articles.excerpt: Andy Burnham backs calls for the return of the 167 bus service from Heywood to Manchester, which was cut in 2012.
articles.content_html:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has backed calls for the reinstatement of the 167 express bus service from Heywood to Manchester, which was discontinued in 2012. The push for its return has been led by Heywood and Middleton MP Elsie Blundell since her election in 2024.

The proposed route would start in Norden, stopping at Bamford, Heywood, and Rhodes before reaching the city centre. Blundell believes that restoring this service would enhance local economic growth and improve transport connectivity for residents.

In a recent House of Commons session, Blundell highlighted that Heywood is the largest town in Greater Manchester without an express bus service to the city centre.

She urged the government to support Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) in delivering this service, which she sees as vital for the community while they await the arrival of Metrolink trams, which are still under consideration.

Burnham criticized the previous Conservative government's decision to deregulate the bus system, stating that it has led to high fares for passengers. He noted that Greater Manchester's public control over buses allows for the introduction of the express service, which he previously supported.

Although current Mayor Bev Craig has not publicly backed the initiative, discussions with Blundell have taken place regarding the express bus and the potential for Metrolink in Heywood.

articles.title: Christmas giving in Rochdale: the toy appeal, the foodbank and the mayor's charities
articles.excerpt: New, unwrapped toys for children aged up to 16 are needed by Friday 11 December, while Rochdale Foodbank is short of juice, rice, toothpaste and coffee.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale borough residents wanting to give this Christmas can help children living in poverty, families relying on food parcels, and the five charities chosen by the mayor.

The borough's Christmas Toy Appeal is collecting gifts until Friday 11 December, so local children living in poverty have a present to open on Christmas Day.

Gifts must be new, not wrapped, and suitable for children up to 16. Organisers say presents for babies and teenagers are especially welcome, because those age groups receive fewer donations.

Gifts can be left during opening hours at any borough library and at venues including Rochdale Leisure Centre, the Crown Oil Arena, Middleton Arena, Heywood Sports Village and Littleborough Sports Centre. They can also be posted to Number One Riverside Giving Back – Christmas Toy Appeal, Number One Riverside, Smith Street, Rochdale OL16 1XU.

The appeal is run by the Number One Riverside Giving Back charity with Rochdale Borough Council, Rochdale AFC, Your Trust and Rochdale Town Centre Management. More than 10,000 toys were donated in 2024, and more than 57,000 since the appeal began in 2014.

Rochdale Foodbank fed 8,444 adults and 4,556 children in 2025, up 13% and 8% on 2024.

Its current shortages are fruit juice, rice, toothpaste, shampoo, treats and coffee. It also lists long-life milk, jam, pasta sauces, tinned fruit, tinned potatoes, sugar, tea bags and cereal as urgent.

Food can be dropped at the warehouse on Newgate, Rochdale, between 10am and midday, Monday to Friday, or at collection points in Tesco on Silk Street, Asda on Dane Street and Morrisons on Kingsway. Money can be given through the foodbank's JustGiving page.

The Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, is raising money this year for Springhill Hospice, The Christie, Sands, Rochdale Veterans' Breakfast Club and Rochdale Women's Welfare Association.

Shoppers can support them at no extra cost by signing up to the Easy Fundraising app, where participating brands donate a share of online purchases. Donations can also be arranged through the Mayor's Office on 01706 924796 or mayoral@rochdale.gov.uk.

articles.title: Police search for man who helped woman after alleged sexual assault in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police are appealing for information regarding a man who assisted a woman following an alleged sexual assault in Rochdale town centre.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester Police are searching for a man who helped a woman following an alleged sexual assault in Rochdale town centre. The incident reportedly occurred at around 4.20am on Saturday, 16 May, in the King Street car park.

Officers stated that the man approached the woman and assisted her in getting home after the incident. Police believe he could be a key witness in their investigation and have issued a social media appeal to identify him.

Police said: "We are looking to identify the man that helped the woman and assisted her in getting home."

The witness was driving a silver Volkswagen Polo and left the scene in the direction of Halifax Road. Police have shared CCTV footage of the vehicle, although they acknowledged the quality is not ideal.

They are urging anyone who recognises the car or has information to come forward.

Anyone with information can contact Greater Manchester Police on 0161 856 4668, quoting the crime reference number CRI/06QQ/0010216/26. Alternatively, information can be submitted online or anonymously through Crimestoppers at 0800 555 111.

articles.title: Christmas lights switch-ons 2026: dates, times and road closures in Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Norden
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton switch on this Saturday 14 November, Rochdale and Norden on Sunday 22 November and Littleborough on Saturday 28 November.
articles.content_html:
Christmas lights will be switched on in Heywood and Middleton this Saturday, with Rochdale, Norden and Littleborough following over the next two weekends.

The dates are Saturday 14 November for Heywood and Middleton, Sunday 22 November for Rochdale town centre and Norden, and Saturday 28 November for Littleborough.

All five events are free. Road closures and parking restrictions apply around each one.

Heywood, Saturday 14 November: the Heywood Christmas Festival takes place in the town centre. Rochdale Borough Council's traffic notice says road closures will be in place from 10am until 6pm, and waiting is banned along the whole of Bethel Street.

A funding report to Heywood Township in the summer proposed a day of family entertainment and fireworks for the switch-on. The switch-on time was not given in the notices seen by Rochdale Daily.

Middleton, Saturday 14 November: the switch-on event is in Middleton Gardens and starts at 12pm, according to the Rochdale Times. It includes food and drink stalls, fairground rides and market stalls, among them the Teenage Market for young traders.

The Art House is hosting Christmas card-making and face painting for children. Middleton Brass Band plays at 4.30pm, before the lights are switched on.

Rochdale town centre, Sunday 22 November: Father Christmas and the Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, will switch on the lights at around 5.30pm in front of Rochdale Town Hall, according to the council.

The switch-on is the final night of the Ignite Fire Festival, which runs from 5pm to 8pm on Friday 20, Saturday 21 and Sunday 22 November in the square and gardens around the town hall, including Broadfield Slopes. Entry is free.

This year's centrepiece is BODY, a night-time trail by outdoor arts company Walk the Plank. The council says it takes visitors through six zones of the human body using fire, light, sound and special effects.

Organisers warn that Ignite includes flashing lights, fire effects, loud noises, smoke and pyrotechnics.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, said: "Ignite is the perfect way to kick off the festive season, bringing together spectacular entertainment, dazzling displays and magical moments for all ages."

Norden, Sunday 22 November: the Norden Christmas lights event is on the same day as the Rochdale switch-on. The council's traffic notice says roads will be closed for the event, with no loading or waiting and no signed alternative route for vehicles. Drivers should check the notice on the council's website for the roads and times.

Littleborough, Saturday 28 November: Church Street will be closed from 1.30pm until 7pm for the Littleborough Christmas Lights Event, according to the council's traffic notice. Waiting is banned from noon until 7pm. The notice does not give the switch-on time.

Later in the season, the borough's Christmas Toy Appeal is collecting new, unwrapped gifts at libraries and leisure centres until Friday 11 December.

Heywood Civic's pantomime this year is Aladdin, and Cinderella opens at Middleton Arena on Sunday 20 December.

At Rochdale Town Hall, Brass and Bublé: A Christmas Special is on Sunday 13 December at 7.15pm, and Jonathan Scott's Christmas organ concert is on Wednesday 16 December.

Rochdale Daily will update this guide as organisers confirm switch-on times.

articles.title: Rochdale’s own Stonehenge? What archaeologists actually know about the moorland stones
articles.excerpt: Surveys and excavations show Bronze Age cairns and widespread prehistoric flint scatters on the moors above Rochdale — but the idea of a local ‘Stonehenge’ is disputed and needs more professional study.
articles.summary: Surveys and excavations show Bronze Age cairns and widespread prehistoric flint scatters on the moors above Rochdale — but the idea of a local ‘Stonehenge’ is disputed and needs more professional study.
articles.body:
On the high ground north of Rochdale, archaeologists have long recorded fragments of a deep past: buried cairns, kerbed barrows and scattered flints that show people were using these uplands from the Mesolithic into the Bronze Age. Recent community fieldwork has pulled those threads together and underlines how the moors are an archaeological patchwork, not a single, tidy monument. ([digventures.com](https://digventures.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/DV_SpoddenValleyRevealed_CommunityArchaeologyReport_v2.0-1.pdf))

That same work also shows why a sensational label — “Rochdale’s Stonehenge” — is misleading. The Spodden Valley Revealed programme, a community archaeology project run with DigVentures, maps Mesolithic and later lithic scatters around Knowl Moor, Brown Wardle and Rooley Moor and records funerary features at places such as Hades Hill and Bagden Hillocks; it also notes a putative Bronze Age stone setting on Hamer Hill, described in earlier records but not settled as a formal monument. ([digventures.com](https://digventures.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/DV_SpoddenValleyRevealed_CommunityArchaeologyReport_v2.0-1.pdf))

There are, however, better-documented prehistoric burials nearby. Wind Hill (Cheesden) is a recognised round-barrow whose excavation by local archaeologists in 1968–72 revealed a slabbed kerb, structural features and grave‑goods consistent with a Beaker‑period burial assemblage. Those finds, now cited in local and regional heritage assessments, are concrete evidence that Bronze Age funerary practices took place on the moors above Rochdale. ([greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk](https://greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/GMCAFiles/PFE/Supporting%20documents/10.06%20Site%20Allocations%20-%20Rochdale/JPA19%20Bamford_Norden/10.06.04%20-%20JPA19%20-%20Bamford_Norden%20Historic%20Environment%20Assessment.pdf))

Claims about new or dramatic stone circles have a short history of being revised after professional survey. Public reports and amateur finds around Hamer Hill and Rooley Moor prompted interest in 2008–09, but a rapid field assessment recorded in monument records noted that much of the visible stonework could be explained by natural blocks or by 19th‑century stone‑working and quarrying associated with local road and sett production. In other words, stones moved or worked in the industrial period can sometimes be mistaken for prehistoric settings. That judgement — recorded in the heritage record summaries — is the reason archaeologists treat the Hamer Hill story cautiously. ([megalithic.co.uk](https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=18858))

That mix of prehistoric deposits and later industrial disturbance is part of the problem for anyone trying to read the surface. The moors were used for quarrying, walling and road‑set production in the 18th–19th centuries; spoil, dressing floors and reused stone can overlay or mimic ancient kerbs and cairns. Good field recording, finds‑analysis and where appropriate small‑scale excavation are the methods specialists use to separate Bronze Age monuments from post‑medieval landscape change. ([megalithic.co.uk](https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=18858))

What the research tells us, plainly, is this: there is established Bronze Age activity on the moors (for example Wind Hill) and a dense scatter of prehistoric flints in museum and survey collections; there are also features that have been proposed as stone settings but which later professional assessment has questioned and in at least one case treated as non‑prehistoric. The Spodden Valley work recommends further targeted survey and community recording to fill the gaps in understanding. ([digventures.com](https://digventures.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/DV_SpoddenValleyRevealed_CommunityArchaeologyReport_v2.0-1.pdf))

For local readers who want to know what happens next: authorities and heritage partners record these places on the local historic environment record and on conservation assessments; community archaeology projects have been used here to consolidate records and to propose routes for better protection and interpretation. Where uncertainty remains — notably the exact nature of the Hamer Hill stones — the responsible course is professional survey rather than publicity. If you are a researcher or landowner seeking the formal record, contact the Greater Manchester HER or the borough’s heritage officers; community groups such as those who worked on Spodden Valley Revealed publish their reports online and welcome archaeological expertise. ([greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk](https://greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/GMCAFiles/PFE/Supporting%20documents/10.06%20Site%20Allocations%20-%20Rochdale/JPA19%20Bamford_Norden/10.06.04%20-%20JPA19%20-%20Bamford_Norden%20Historic%20Environment%20Assessment.pdf))

Finally, a practical note: these moorland sites are sensitive. Precise locations of vulnerable or unprotected sites are normally handled through the local HER and museum services rather than shouted from the hillsides; that helps protect fragile features from inadvertent damage. The clearest picture of “what happened” on our moors comes from combining older excavations (for example the Wind Hill cairn), modern survey, and careful community recording — not from a single photograph or a nickname. ([greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk](https://greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/GMCAFiles/PFE/Supporting%20documents/10.06%20Site%20Allocations%20-%20Rochdale/JPA19%20Bamford_Norden/10.06.04%20-%20JPA19%20-%20Bamford_Norden%20Historic%20Environment%20Assessment.pdf))

articles.title: Rochdale Council reminds parents of primary school application deadline
articles.excerpt: Parents must apply for their child's primary school place by 15 January 2027 to secure their preferred choice, warns Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has issued a reminder to parents that the deadline for applying for primary school places is 15 January 2027. This notice is particularly aimed at parents of children who will be starting school in September 2027.

In 2026, 216 parents submitted late applications for primary school places, and 37% of those children missed out on their first preferred school. In contrast, 89% of on-time applicants secured their preferred choice, highlighting the importance of timely applications.

Councillor Rachel Massey emphasized that while the deadline may seem distant, it is approaching quickly. She stated that late applications can significantly impact school placements and urged parents to apply on time to avoid disappointment.

The council's reminder serves as a crucial prompt for parents to ensure they do not miss the application window, which could affect their children's educational opportunities.

Published: 12 November 2026 Parents who have children starting primary school next September are being reminded to apply for their child’s school place before Friday 15 January 2027. While the New Year deadline feels quite a distance away to some, data held by Rochdale Borough Council shows families still miss this important deadline. In 2026, 216 parents submitted a late primary school application. This led to more than a third of those children (37%) missing out on their first preferred school as a result when reception started this September. In comparison, 89% of those who submitted an application on time secured their preferred school. Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, said: “We know life is busy for families, especially when your children are a lot younger, but it is so important to get your school applications in on time. “While the deadline is in the New Year, January will be here before we know it, so I urge all families to get their applications in as soon as they can to give your child the best possible chance of securing their preferred primary school.” Families must complete their primary school application through the local authority’s online parent portal. This includes families who have children that already attend a school nursery, as there is no automatic transition from nursery to reception. Parents are advised to make 5 preferences as part of their application and to avoid duplicating or selecting only one preference as this will not increase their chances of obtaining a place at any school. Before making any decision, families are encouraged to gather as much information on their preferred schools as they can. This could include reading the respective admissions criteria, prospectus and Ofsted report of each school. It could also include arranging a visit to their preferred schools as part of any upcoming open evenings, or by arranging a direct visit with the school if they cannot attend their opening events. Parents should also consider whether the distance to the school will affect their chances of being allocated a place, how it will impact how their child travels to school and if this could be a problem if their child was to take part in after school activities. articles.title: Krisnan Inu appointed assistant coach of Rochdale Hornets
articles.excerpt: Krisnan Inu has been appointed as the new assistant coach for Rochdale Hornets as they prepare for the 2027 season.
articles.content_html:
Krisnan Inu has been appointed as the new assistant coach of Rochdale Hornets, a significant development as the club prepares for the 2027 season.

Inu, who has played for various clubs across Australia, New Zealand, England, and France, previously served as an assistant coach at Salford Red Devils. His experience in both playing and coaching is expected to bring valuable insights to the Hornets' coaching staff.

Expressing his enthusiasm for the role, Inu said he is excited to start working with the coaching staff and players, aiming to contribute both on and off the field for the club.

As preparations for the upcoming season get underway, the Hornets will be looking to leverage Inu's expertise to enhance their performance in the league.

articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council lists work affecting Cartridge Street in Heywood; expected timings: The closure began at 10.29am on Wednesday, 11 November 2026. Work will continue for a maximum of 21 days (2 December 2026), or when repairs are complete if sooner..
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has published a traffic notice for Cartridge Street in Heywood. The council lists the expected start and finish as The closure began at 10.29am on Wednesday, 11 November 2026. Work will continue for a maximum of 21 days (2 December 2026), or when repairs are complete if sooner..

The council gives the reason as To repair a leaking service in the road. The notice describes the affected area as follows: Part of Cartridge Street has been temporarily closed.

The closure begins at the junction with Coomassie Street and ends 110 metres along the road in a westerly direction.

The published alternative route is Coomassie Street, Egerton Street, Pilsworth Road, Tower Street and Cartridge Street. These are the details in the council's current published record, rather than confirmation that work has started or finished. Readers travelling through the area can check the original Rochdale Borough Council notice for any subsequent amendments.

articles.title: Springhill Hospice appeals for volunteers to collect Christmas trees in January
articles.excerpt: Springhill Hospice needs volunteers and drivers with vans or trucks for its Christmas tree recycling collections from Friday 15 to Monday 18 January 2027.
articles.content_html:
Springhill Hospice needs volunteers and van drivers to help collect hundreds of real Christmas trees from homes across Rochdale borough in January.

The Rochdale hospice is looking for helpers for its 2027 Christmas tree recycling scheme, run in partnership with the charity JustHelping, which raises money for local hospice care.

Collections will run from 8am on Friday 15 January to Monday 18 January 2027, covering the OL10, OL11, OL12, OL15, OL16 and M24 postcode areas.

The hospice is particularly keen to hear from volunteer drivers and from anyone who can lend a van, truck or other larger vehicle for collections.

Springhill provides care for adults with a life-limiting condition, and for their loved ones, across Heywood, Middleton and Rochdale.

Victoria Barnett, senior corporate fundraiser at Springhill Hospice, said: “Our Christmas tree recycling scheme is only made possible thanks to the incredible volunteers and local businesses who give their time and energy to help us collect hundreds of trees.

“We’d love to hear from anyone in Heywood, Middleton and Rochdale who could help us this year. It’s a fantastic way to start the new year, get involved in the local community and make a real difference to the care we provide for local people and their families.”

Last year, 10 volunteers and six businesses helped collect 200 real Christmas trees from homes across the borough, and Special Branch Tree Surgeons Ltd chipped them.

The chippings were used on pathways around the hospice, and donations from the scheme raised £3,215 for local hospice care.

This year’s scheme is sponsored by Target Fire Protection. The hospice says all money raised will help it care for people affected by life-limiting illness and bereavement.

Anyone interested in volunteering can contact Ami Wegrzyn, corporate fundraiser at Springhill, by emailing Ami.Wegrzyn@springhill.org.uk. Households wishing to book a tree collection can do so through Springhill Hospice’s website.

Source: Springhill Hospice press release supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph: Springhill Hospice / supplied.

articles.title: Super Stories with Eliza Says launches at Alkrington Library
articles.excerpt: Alkrington Library will host 'Super Stories with Eliza Says', a new children's event featuring songs and British Sign Language, starting this month.
articles.content_html:
Alkrington Library will host 'Super Stories with Eliza Says', a new children's event that combines storytelling, fun songs, and simple British Sign Language, starting this month.

The sessions are designed for families with children aged 0–5, featuring a collection of 30 timeless picture books. This initiative aims to promote literacy and engagement among young readers in the community.

Rochdale Borough Council stated that the first sessions will take place at Alkrington, Littleborough, and Castleton libraries on 17 November 2026, with plans to expand to Middleton, Heywood, Spotland, Balderstone, and Langley libraries in 2027.

Part of Ramsden Road in Wardle will be closed on Christmas Eve for the Wardle Village Christmas Eve Carol Concert.

The road will be closed between its junctions with Crossfield Road and Wardle Fold from 5.30pm to 7.30pm on Thursday 24 December 2026.

Rochdale Borough Council, which is organising the closure, says there will be no alternative route for vehicles.

The council's notice, with directions and a map of roadworks across Greater Manchester, is on the Rochdale Borough Council website.
